**디자인하다** (dijainhada) = to design — **디자인** (design loanword) + **하다**.
**디자인** alone = design (noun): **디자인이 예뻐요** = 'the design is pretty'.
**웹사이트** (wepsaiteu) = website — loanword from English.
**그래픽 디자이너** (graepik dijaino) = graphic designer — a common loanword profession title.

**팔다** (palda) = to sell — an irregular ㄹ verb: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/시.
**팔아요** = polite present; **팔았어요** = past tense.
**자동차** (jadongcha) = car — Sino-Korean: **자** (自, self) + **동** (動, move) + **차** (車, vehicle).
Opposite: **사다** (sada) = to buy.

**사다** (sada) = to buy — a simple vowel-stem verb.
**사야 해요** = 'must buy' — **-아야 하다** expresses obligation: **사다** → **사야 해요**.
**컴퓨터** (keompyuteo) = computer — loanword.
**새** (sae) = new (used only as a modifier before nouns, not as a predicate); **새 컴퓨터** = new computer.
cards.englishPhrase: I need to buy a new computer.

cards.grammarNote:
**돕다** (dopda) = to help — irregular ㅂ verb: **도와요** (help), **도왔어요** (helped).
**도와드릴까요?** = 'shall I help you?' — **도와드리다** is the humble/honorific form: 'help (upward)'.
**드리다** (deurida) = humble form of **주다** (give) — used when giving/offering to a superior.
Compare: **도와줄까요?** (shall I help you? — equal level) vs. **도와드릴까요?** (shall I help you? — respectful).

**관리하다** (gwallihada) = to manage/administer — Sino-Korean: **관리** (管理, management) + **하다**.
**관리** alone = management (noun): **관리가 필요해요** = 'management is needed'.
**팀을 관리하다** = to manage a team — **을** = object marker after a consonant.
**관리자** (gwallija) = manager/administrator — the person who does **관리**.

**만나다** (mannada) = to meet — a simple vowel-stem verb: **만나요** (meet), **만났어요** (met).
**만남** (mannam) = a meeting/encounter — the noun form of **만나다**.
**매주** (maeju) = every week — **매주 월요일에** = 'every Monday'.
**처음 뵙겠습니다** = 'nice to meet you (for the first time)' — the formal first-meeting phrase.

**시작하다** (sijaghada) = to start/begin — **시작** (始作, start) + **하다**.
**시작하다** is transitive (takes an object): **일을 시작해요** = 'start work'.
**시작되다** (sijakdoeda) = to begin (intransitive/passive): **회의가 시작돼요** = 'the meeting starts'.
**여덟 시에** = 'at eight o'clock' — native Korean number **여덟** (eight) + **시** (時, o'clock) + **에**.

**끝나다** (kkeunnada) = to end/finish (intransitive) — 'the work ends'.
**끝내다** (kkeunnaeda) = to finish/complete (transitive) — 'I finish the work'.
**일이 끝나요** = 'work ends' — **이** = subject marker after a consonant.
**퇴근하다** (toegeunhada) = to leave work — a more specific and commonly used workplace verb.

**좋아하다** = to like.
Liking a thing: **X를/을 좋아해요** (I like X).
Liking an activity: **X하는 걸 좋아해요** (I like doing X).
**즐기다** = to enjoy (implies stronger, more active enjoyment).
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading. She likes singing.

cards.grammarNote:
**쉬다** (swida) = to rest/relax — a basic, essential verb.
**쉬어요** = polite present; **쉬었어요** = past tense.
**휴식을 취하다** (hyusigeul chwihada) = to take a rest — more formal expression.
**주말에 쉬어요** = 'I rest on weekends' — **에** after **주말** marks a recurring time.

**스트레스** (seuteuresse) is a loanword from English.
**스트레스가 많다** = 'there is a lot of stress' — **가** = subject marker after a vowel.
**스트레스를 받다** = 'to receive/feel stress' — a common fixed expression.
**스트레스가 많은** = modifier form: **스트레스가 많은 일** (stressful work).

**행복하다** = to be happy (deep, lasting happiness) → **행복해요**.
**기쁘다** = to be glad/delighted (in the moment) → **기뻐요**.
Korean emotions are adjectives that become predicates directly.

**슬픈** (seulpeun) is the adjective modifier form of **슬프다** (seulpeuda, to be sad).
**슬프다** → **슬퍼요** (seulpeoyo) in polite speech — irregular ㅡ drop before vowel endings.
Related noun: **슬픔** (seulpeum) = sadness.
Use **슬퍼요** as a predicate: **왜 슬퍼요?** = Why are you sad?

**사랑** (sarang) is a pure Korean noun meaning love.
The verb form is **사랑하다** (saranghada) → **사랑해요** (saranghaeyo) in polite speech.
**사랑을 느껴요** = I feel love — **을** (eul) is the object particle after a consonant-final noun.
Contrast **사랑** (romantic/deep love) with **좋아함** (joaham, liking/fondness).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel a lot of love for my family.

cards.grammarNote:
**화** (hwa) = anger/fire; a short pure Korean noun.
The idiom **화가 나다** (hwa-ga nada) literally means 'anger rises/comes out' — **가** is the subject particle.
**화가 났어요** = I got angry (past tense: **나다** → **났어요**).
Stronger synonym: **분노** (bunno) — Sino-Korean for wrath/fury.
cards.englishPhrase: I felt anger when they lied to me.

cards.grammarNote:
**두려움** (duryeoum) is the noun form of **두렵다** (duryeopda, to be fearful) — the ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 워 before vowels.
**두렵다** → **두려워요** (duryeowoyo) in polite speech.
Related: **무섭다** (museopda) = to be scary/scared → **무서워요** (museowoyo).
**두려움** vs **공포** (gongpo): **두려움** is personal dread; **공포** (Sino-Korean) is terror/horror.

**희망** (huimang) is Sino-Korean: 希望 — hope/wish.
As a verb: **희망하다** (huimanghada) → **희망해요**; in everyday speech **바라다** (barada) is more natural.
**희망이 있어요** = there is hope — **이** (i) is the subject particle after consonant **망**.
Contrast **희망** (long-term hope) with **기대** (gidae, expectation/anticipation).
cards.englishPhrase: I have hope for the future.

cards.grammarNote:
**스트레스** (seuteurese) is a loanword from English 'stress'.
Common phrase: **스트레스를 받다** (seuteurese-reul batda) = to receive/get stress.
**스트레스가 많아요** = I have a lot of stress — **가** is the subject particle; **많다** (manta) = to be many/much.
Related: **스트레스를 풀다** (seuteurese-reul pulda) = to relieve stress.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of stress at work.

cards.grammarNote:
**기분** (gibun) is Sino-Korean: 氣分 — lit. 'energy-portion'; mood/feeling.
**기분이 좋아요** = I'm in a good mood (lit. 'my mood is good') — **이** is the subject particle.
Korean describes mood states as noun + adjective rather than verb: **기분이 나빠요** = I'm in a bad mood.
Related: **기분 전환** (gibun jeonhwan) = mood change/a change of pace.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a good mood today.

cards.grammarNote:
**감정** (gamjeong) is Sino-Korean: 感情 — emotion/feeling (the full range of emotions).
Distinct from **기분** (gibun, momentary mood) — **감정** refers to deeper emotional states.
**감정이에요** = it is an emotion — **이에요** is the copula after a consonant-final noun.
Related: **감정적** (gamjeongjeok) = emotional (adjective); **감정을 숨기다** = to hide one's feelings.

**감동** (gamdong) = being moved/touched emotionally — Sino-Korean 感動.
Note the phrase uses **감동** (deep emotional impact) rather than plain **감정** (emotion).
**숨길 수 없었어요** = could not hide — **-ㄹ/을 수 없다** means 'cannot' + past tense **-었어요**.
**감동받다** (gamdong batda) = to be moved/touched; **감동시키다** = to move someone emotionally.

**침착함** (chimchakam) is the nominalized form of **침착하다** (chimchakada, to be composed/calm).
Nominalization: **침착하다** + **-ㅁ** → **침착함** (noun: composure).
**침착함을 유지하다** = to maintain composure — **을** is the object particle; **유지하다** = to maintain.
Related: **침착하게** (chimchakage) = calmly (adverb form).

**걱정** (geokjeong) = worry/concern — pure Korean noun.
Verb form: **걱정하다** (geokjeonghada) → **걱정해요** in polite speech.
**걱정 때문에** = because of worry — **때문에** (ttaemune) expresses cause/reason.
**걱정하지 마세요** = please don't worry — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.

**놀라움** (nollaum) is the noun form of **놀랍다** (nollapda, to be surprising) — ㅂ irregular.
**놀랍다** → **놀라워요** (nollawoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
The verb **놀라다** (nollada) = to be startled/surprised → **놀랐어요** (past: I was surprised).
Contrast: **놀람** (nollam) = sudden shock; **놀라움** = a sense of wonder/amazement.

**증오** (jeungo) is Sino-Korean: 憎惡 — intense hatred/loathing.
Verb form: **증오하다** (jeungohada) → **증오해요**.
Milder everyday word: **싫다** (silta) = to dislike → **싫어요** (sireoyo).
**감정이에요** = it is an emotion — **이에요** is the polite copula after consonant-final nouns.

**고통** (gotong) is Sino-Korean: 苦痛 — suffering/anguish (emotional or physical).
Physical pain is also **통증** (tongjeung, 痛症) — specifically a medical ache.
**느껴져요** = is felt — passive form of **느끼다** using **-아/어지다** construction.
Related: **고통스럽다** (gotongseureupda) = to be painful/agonizing → **고통스러워요** (ㅂ irregular).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel pain in my leg.

cards.grammarNote:
**에너지** (eneoji) is a loanword from English 'energy'.
Native Korean equivalent: **기운** (gieun) = vitality/vigor/energy.
**에너지가 넘쳐요** = energy overflows — **넘치다** (neomchida) = to overflow/be full of.
**가** is the subject particle after the vowel-final **에너지**.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of energy today.

cards.grammarNote:
**느끼다** = to feel/sense something.
**기분이 좋아요** = I feel good (lit. 'my mood is good').
Korean often expresses emotional states as noun + adjective: **기분** (mood/feeling) + state adjective, rather than using a verb.

**사랑하다** (saranghada) = to love — **사랑** (noun) + **하다** (to do) compound verb.
**사랑하다** → **사랑해요** (saranghaeyo) in polite speech — **하다** → **해요**.
**당신** (dangsin) = you (formal/written); in speech, names or **너** (neo, informal) are more natural.
**많이** (manhi) = a lot/much — adverb from **많다** (to be many).

**싫어하다** (sireohada) = to hate/dislike — from **싫다** (silta, to be unpleasant) + **-어하다**.
**싫어하다** → **싫어해요** (sireohaeyo) in polite speech.
**기다리는 걸** = waiting [object] — **-는** nominalizes the verb; **걸** = **것을** (thing/act + obj particle).
Distinct from **증오하다** (jeungohada): **싫어하다** = general dislike; **증오하다** = deep hatred.

**좋아하다** (joahada) = to like — from the adjective **좋다** (jota, to be good) + **-아하다**.
**좋아하다** → **좋아해요** (joahaeyo) in polite speech.
Contrast **좋다** (jota, it is good/I like it — stative) with **좋아하다** (active feeling of liking).
**음악을 좋아해요** = I like music — **을** is the object particle after consonant-final **악**.

**즐기다** (jeulgida) = to enjoy — pure Korean verb.
**즐기다** → **즐겨요** (jeulgyeoyo) in polite speech — ㅣ stem drops before 어: **기** → **겨**.
Related: **즐거운** (jeulgeoun) = fun/enjoyable (adjective); **즐거움** (jeulgeoum) = enjoyment (noun).
**주말을 즐겨요** = I enjoy the weekend — **을** is the object particle.

**두려워하다** (duryeowohada) = to fear — **두렵다** (adjective) + **-어하다** → action verb.
**두려워하다** → **두려워해요** (duryeowohaeyo) in polite speech.
The ㅂ irregular: **두렵다** → **두려워** before vowels — ㅂ changes to 워.
**최악의 상황** = the worst situation — **최악** (choerak, 最惡) is Sino-Korean for 'worst'.

**바라다** (barada) = to wish/hope — pure Korean verb, more heartfelt than **희망하다**.
**바라다** → **바라요** (barayo) in polite speech — vowel stem, so -아요 is added.
**되길 바라요** = I hope it goes well — **-길** is a shortening of **-기를** (nominalizer + object particle).
Related pattern: **-기를 바라다** = to hope that... (formal written form).

**걱정하다** (geokjeonghada) = to worry — **걱정** (noun) + **하다** (to do).
**걱정하다** → **걱정해요** in polite speech; **걱정하지 마세요** = please don't worry.
**그것에 대해** = about that — **에 대해** (e daehae) is a fixed phrase meaning 'regarding/about'.
**마세요** = please don't — the polite negative imperative form, from **말다** (malda, to stop/refrain).

**평화** (pyeonghwa) is Sino-Korean: 平和 — peace/harmony.
Adjective form: **평화롭다** (pyeonghwaropda) → **평화로워요** (pyeonghwarowoyo) — ㅂ irregular.
**고요함** (goyoham) = quietness/stillness, nominalized from **고요하다** (goyohada).
**와/과** (wa/gwa) = and/with — **평화와** uses **와** after the vowel-final **화**.

**질투** (jiltu) is Sino-Korean: 嫉妬 — jealousy/envy.
Verb form: **질투하다** (jiltuhada) → **질투해요**; **질투나다** = to feel jealous (jealousy arises).
Related: **부러움** (bureouм) = envy (wanting what another has); **질투** focuses on rivalry.
**는** (neun) after **질투** is the topic particle — used here to make a general statement.

**짜증** (jjajeung) = annoyance/irritation — pure Korean noun.
**짜증이 나다** (jjajeungi nada) = annoyance arises; **짜증나게 하다** = to make [something] annoying.
In speech, **짜증 나요** (jjajeung nayo) is most natural: lit. 'annoyance comes out'.
**소음** (soeum, 騷音) = noise — Sino-Korean: **소** (noise) + **음** (sound).

**화나게 하다** (hwanage hada) = to anger — **화나다** (to become angry) + **-게 하다** (causative).
**화가 나다** = anger arises (intransitive); **화나게 하다** = to cause anger in someone (transitive).
**했어요** is the polite past tense of **하다**: **하다** → **했어요**.
**말** (mal) = words/speech — particle **이** (subject) follows consonant-final **말**.

**미소** (miso) = smile — Sino-Korean: 微笑 (slight smile).
**미소 짓다** (miso jitda) = to smile — lit. 'to make/form a smile'; **짓다** = to make/build.
**미소 지어요** (miso jieoyo) is the polite present — **짓다** has the ㅅ irregular: ㅅ drops before vowels.
Related: **웃다** (utda) = to laugh/smile broadly; **미소** is specifically a gentle smile.

**웃다** (utda) = to laugh/smile — pure Korean verb.
**웃다** → **웃어요** (useoyo) in polite speech — the ㅅ irregular: ㅅ drops before vowel endings.
Past tense: **웃었어요** (uteosseoyo) = laughed.
Related: **웃음** (useum) = laughter/smile (noun); **웃기다** (utgida) = to be funny.

**울다** (ulda) = to cry/weep — pure Korean verb with ㄹ stem.
**울다** → **울어요** (ureoyo) in polite present; **ㄹ** drops before certain endings but stays before 어.
Progressive: **울고 있어요** = is crying — **-고 있다** expresses ongoing action.
Related: **울음** (ureum) = crying (noun); **눈물** (nunmul) = tears (lit. eye-water).

**소리치다** (sorichida) = to shout/scream — compound: **소리** (sori, sound/voice) + **치다** (to strike/do).
**소리치지 마세요** = please don't shout — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.
Related: **소리 지르다** (sori jireuda) = to scream loudly; **외치다** (oechida) = to cry out/exclaim.
**소리** alone = sound/noise; **목소리** (moksori) = voice (lit. throat-sound).

**쉬다** (swida) = to rest/relax/breathe — pure Korean verb.
The phrase uses **긴장을 풀다** instead — lit. 'to undo/release tension' — a more natural expression.
**긴장** (ginжang, 緊張) = tension — Sino-Korean; **풀다** (pulda) = to release/solve/undo.
**급하지 않아요** = it's not urgent — **급하다** (geupada) = to be urgent/hurried; **-지 않아요** = negation.

**화가 난** (hwa-ga nan) = angry — lit. 'anger has risen'; noun modifier form of **화가 나다**.
**화가 나다** → past modifier **화가 난** (anger-has-risen), used before nouns.
As predicate: **화가 났어요** = I got/am angry — **났어요** is past tense of **나다** (to arise).
**에게** (ege) = to/toward a person: **당신에게 화가 났어요** = I'm angry at you.

**무서운** (museoun) is the adjective modifier form of **무섭다** (museopda, to be scary/scared).
**무섭다** → **무서워요** (museowoyo) in polite speech — ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 워 before vowels.
For expressing personal fear: **무섭다** = it is scary (to me); **두렵다** = I dread/fear it.
**무서워했어요** = was scared — **-어하다** turns an adjective into an active emotional verb (past tense).

**불안한** (buranhan) is the adjective modifier of **불안하다** (buranhada, to be anxious/uneasy).
**불안** (buran) is Sino-Korean: 不安 — lit. 'not-safe'; unease/anxiety.
**불안해요** (buranhaeyo) = I'm anxious — **하다** adjective → **해요** in polite speech.
Related: **불안감** (burangam) = a feeling of anxiety; **불안정** (buranjeong) = instability.

**긴장된** (ginжangdoen) = nervous/tensed — **긴장** (tension) + **된** (become, past passive modifier).
**긴장하다** (ginжanghada) = to become tense/nervous; **긴장돼요** = I'm nervous (contraction of **되어요**).
**긴장** (緊張) is Sino-Korean — lit. 'tight-stretch'; commonly used for pre-event nerves.
Contrast with **불안하다** (anxiety) — **긴장하다** is often situational/performance nerves.

**신이 난** (sini nan) = excited — lit. 'spirit/energy has risen'; **신** (spirit/enthusiasm) + **이 나다**.
The phrase uses **기대돼요** = I'm looking forward to it — **기대** (gidae, 期待) = expectation.
**기대되다** = to be anticipated — **되다** suffix makes a passive/spontaneous feeling verb.
Contrast: **신이 나다** (energetic excitement) vs **설레다** (fluttery/romantic anticipation).

**즐거운** (jeulgoun) is the adjective modifier of **즐겁다** (jeulgeopda, to be fun/joyful) — ㅂ irregular.
**즐겁다** → **즐거워요** (jeulgeoweoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
The phrase uses **명랑하다** (myeongnanghada) — more specifically cheerful/bright in personality.
**항상** (hangsang) = always — adverb used with habitual present tense.

**자랑스러운** is the modifier form of **자랑스럽다** (jarangseureupda, to be proud) — ㅂ irregular.
**자랑스럽다** → **자랑스러워요** (jarangseureoweoyo) in polite speech.
**자랑** (jarang) = boast/pride (noun); **-스럽다** suffix = -ful/-ish (creates descriptive adjective).
**당신이 자랑스러워요** = I'm proud of you — the person you're proud of takes **이/가** (subject particle).

**만족한** is the modifier of **만족하다** (manjokada, to be satisfied/content) — Sino-Korean 滿足.
**만족하다** → **만족해요** (manjokaeyo) in polite speech.
**에 만족하다** = to be satisfied with — **에** (e) marks the thing one is content with.
Related: **만족감** (manjokgam) = a sense of satisfaction; **불만족** (bulmanjok) = dissatisfaction.

**침착한** (chimchakhan) is the modifier form of **침착하다** (chimchakada, to be composed/calm).
**침착하세요** = Please stay calm — **-하세요** is the polite imperative of **하다** adjectives.
**괜찮아요** (gwaenchanhayo) = it's fine/okay — a very common reassurance phrase.
**다** (da) = all/everything — short adverb meaning 'completely' or 'all is'.

**스트레스받는** = stress-receiving — compound modifier: **스트레스** + **받다** (batda, to receive) + **-는**.
**스트레스를 받다** = to be stressed/get stressed (lit. 'to receive stress').
The phrase uses **스트레스가 많아요** = there is a lot of stress — subject + **많다** (to be much).
**이번 주** (ibeon ju) = this week — **이번** (this time/this) + **주** (week, Sino-Korean 週).

**압도된** (apdo-doen) = overwhelmed — **압도** (apdo, 壓倒, to overwhelm) + **된** (passive past modifier).
**압도되다** (apdo-doeda) = to be overwhelmed — **되다** makes it passive/spontaneous.
**느낌이에요** = it's a feeling — **느낌** (neukkum, feeling/sense) + copula **이에요**.
Related: **벅차다** (beokchada) = to feel overwhelmed/welling up — a more emotional pure Korean word.
cards.englishPhrase: I feel overwhelmed by the work.

cards.grammarNote:
**활기찬** (hwalgichan) = energetic/lively — compound: **활기** (hwalgi, vitality) + **차다** (to be full of).
**활기** is Sino-Korean: 活氣 — lit. 'living-energy'; vibrancy/liveliness.
**활기차다** → **활기차요** (hwalgichayo) in polite speech.
Related: **활발하다** (hwalbalada) = to be active/lively; **생기** (saenggi) = vitality/freshness.

**피곤한** (pigonhan) is the modifier form of **피곤하다** (pigonhada, to be tired) — Sino-Korean 疲困.
**피곤하다** → **피곤해요** (pigonhaeyo) in polite speech.
Related pure Korean word: **지치다** (jichida) = to be worn out/exhausted → **지쳐요** (jichyeoyo).
**너무** (neomu) = too/very — intensifier: **너무 피곤해요** = I'm very tired.

**지친** (jichin) is the past modifier of **지치다** (jichida, to be exhausted/worn out) — pure Korean.
**지치다** → **지쳐요** (jichyeoyo) in polite present; **지쳤어요** (jichyeosseoyo) = (I am) exhausted (past).
**완전히** (wanjeonhi) = completely/totally — adverb from **완전하다** (wanjeonhada, to be complete).
Related: **기진맥진하다** (gijinmaekjinhada) = to be utterly exhausted (more emphatic/formal expression).

**궁금한** (gunggeumhan) is the modifier of **궁금하다** (gunggeumhada, to be curious/wondering).
**궁금하다** → **궁금해요** (gunggeumhaeyo) in polite speech.
**궁금하다** is used when you are wondering about something specific: **그게 궁금해요** = I'm curious about that.
Related: **호기심** (hogisim, 好奇心) = curiosity (the feeling itself) — Sino-Korean noun.

Pain is expressed with **아프다** (to hurt/be sick).
The body part takes the subject particle **이/가**: **머리가 아파요** = my head hurts.
This construction is used for all body pain.

**머리카락** (meorikaraк) = hair strand — compound: **머리** (head) + **카락** (strand/piece).
**머리** alone can mean both 'head' and 'hair' in casual speech; **머리카락** is specifically a hair strand.
**머리카락이 길어요** = her hair is long — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **락**.
**길다** (gilda) = to be long → **길어요** (gireoyo) in polite speech (ㄹ stem + 어요).

**얼굴** (eolgul) = face — pure Korean noun.
**얼굴을 씻다** = to wash one's face — **씻다** (ssitda) = to wash; **을** is the object particle.
**씻으세요** = please wash — **씻다** + **으세요** (polite imperative after consonant-final stem).
Related: **얼굴색** (eolgulsaek) = facial complexion; **인상** (insang) = facial impression.

**눈** (nun) = eye — pure Korean; also means 'snow' (same spelling, different context).
Korean does not mark grammatical plurality: **눈** = eye or eyes depending on context.
**눈을 감다** = to close one's eyes; **눈을 뜨다** = to open one's eyes.
Related compound: **눈물** (nunmul) = tears (lit. eye-water); **눈썹** (nunsseop) = eyebrow.

**귀** (gwi) = ear — pure Korean noun.
**귀가 아파요** = my ear hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **귀**.
Pain expression pattern: body part + **이/가** + **아파요** (from **아프다**, to hurt/be sick).
Related: **귀걸이** (gwigeolli) = earring (lit. ear-hanger); **귀머거리** = deaf person (informal/old).

**코** (ko) = nose — pure Korean noun.
**코가 차가워요** = my nose is cold — **가** is the subject particle; **차갑다** (chagapda) = to be cold (to the touch).
**차갑다** → **차가워요** (chagawoyo) in polite speech — ㅂ irregular.
Related: **코막힘** (komakiм) = nasal congestion (lit. nose-blockage); **콧물** (konmul) = runny nose/mucus.

**입** (ip) = mouth — pure Korean noun.
**입을 벌리다** = to open one's mouth — **벌리다** (beollida) = to spread apart/open wide.
**벌리세요** = please open — **벌리다** + **세요** (polite imperative after vowel-final stem).
Related: **입술** (ipsul) = lips; **입맛** (immат) = taste/appetite (lit. mouth-taste).

**입술** (ipsul) = lip/lips — compound: **입** (ip, mouth) + **술** (old word for edge/border).
Korean uses the same word **입술** for one lip or both lips — number is inferred from context.
**빨갛다** (ppalgatda) = to be red → **빨개요** (ppalg aeyo) in polite speech — ㅎ irregular.
**이** after **입술** is the subject particle (consonant-final **술**).

**이** (i) = tooth/teeth — pure Korean; same as the subject particle **이**, so context is key.
**이가 아파요** = I have a toothache (lit. 'tooth hurts') — the subject particle **가** follows vowel-final **이**.
Alternative word: **치아** (chia, 齒牙) — Sino-Korean, used in formal/medical contexts (e.g. at the dentist).
Related: **이를 닦다** (ireul dakda) = to brush one's teeth; **충치** (chungchi) = cavity (Sino-Korean).

**혀** (hyeo) = tongue — pure Korean noun.
**혀를 내밀다** = to stick out one's tongue — **내밀다** (naemilda) = to extend/stick out.
**내미세요** = please stick out — polite imperative; **를** is the object particle after vowel-final **혀**.
Related: **혓바늘** (hyeotbaneul) = tongue sore/ulcer; **혀가 꼬이다** = to get tongue-tied.

**목** (mok) = neck — pure Korean; also means 'throat' in some contexts.
**목이 뻣뻣해요** = my neck is stiff — **이** is the subject particle; **뻣뻣하다** = to be stiff/rigid.
**목소리** (moksori) = voice — compound: **목** (throat) + **소리** (sound).
For throat pain: **목이 아파요** = my throat hurts; **목감기** (mokkamgi) = throat cold.

**팔** (pal) = arm — pure Korean noun (also means 'eight' — a homonym).
**팔이 골절됐어요** = I broke my arm — **골절** (goljeol, 骨折) = fracture; Sino-Korean.
**골절되다** (goljeol-doeda) = to be fractured — **되다** makes it passive; past: **됐어요**.
Related: **팔꿈치** (palkkumchi) = elbow; **오른팔** (oreunpal) = right arm (compound).

**손** (son) = hand/hands — pure Korean; no plural marking needed in Korean.
**손을 씻다** = to wash one's hands — **씻다** (ssitda) = to wash; **을** is the object particle.
Compounds: **손가락** (songarak) = finger (hand-branch); **손목** (sonmok) = wrist (hand-neck).
Related: **악수하다** (aksuhada) = to shake hands — Sino-Korean 握手.

**손가락** (songarak) = finger — compound: **손** (son, hand) + **가락** (garak, long slender object).
Toe is **발가락** (balgarak): **발** (bal, foot) + **가락** — parallel compound structure.
**베다** (beda) = to cut/slice; **베었어요** = cut (past tense) — **베다** + **었어요**.
Finger joints: **손가락 마디** (songarak madi); fingernail: **손톱** (sontop, hand-shell).

**가슴** (gaseum) = chest — pure Korean; covers both chest and breast/heart area emotionally.
**가슴이 아파요** = chest hurts — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **슴**.
**가슴이 뛰다** = heart is beating/chest is pounding — idiomatic for excitement or fear.
Medical term for chest: **흉부** (hyungbu, 胸部) — Sino-Korean used in clinical settings.

**등** (deung) = back (of the body) — pure Korean noun.
**등이 아파요** = my back hurts — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **등**.
Lower back is **허리** (heori); **등** refers specifically to the upper/mid back.
Related: **등뼈** (deungppyeo) = spine (lit. back-bone); **척추** (cheokchu) = spine (Sino-Korean medical term).

**어깨** (eokkae) = shoulder — pure Korean noun.
**어깨가 아파요** = my shoulder hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **어깨**.
Idiom: **어깨가 무겁다** = to feel a heavy burden (lit. shoulders are heavy) — figurative use.
Related: **어깨동무** (eokkaedongmu) = putting arms around each other's shoulders (friendship gesture).

**팔꿈치** (palkkumchi) = elbow — compound: **팔** (pal, arm) + **꿈치** (kkumchi, bent tip/end).
Parallel to **발꿈치** (balkkumchi) = heel — **꿈치** is the pure Korean word for a protrusion/tip.
**팔꿈치가 아파요** = my elbow hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **치**.
Related: **팔씨름** (palssireum) = arm wrestling; **팔꿈치를 짚다** = to prop oneself on one's elbow.

**무릎** (mureup) = knee — pure Korean noun.
**무릎을 다치다** = to hurt one's knee — **다치다** (dachida) = to get hurt; **을** is the object particle.
**무릎을 꿇다** (mureupеul kkultda) = to kneel (lit. to bend the knee) — a common idiom.
Related: **무릎뼈** (mureupppyeo) = kneecap; **슬개골** (seulgaegol) = patella (Sino-Korean medical term).

**다리** (dari) = leg — pure Korean noun; also means 'bridge' (same spelling, different context).
**다리가 피곤해요** = my legs are tired — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **다리**.
**피곤하다** (pigonhada) = to be tired/fatigued — Sino-Korean 疲困 → **피곤해요**.
Related: **다리뼈** (darippyeo) = leg bone; **무릎** (mureup) = knee; **발** (bal) = foot.

**발** (bal) = foot/feet — pure Korean; no separate plural form in Korean.
**발이 아파요** = my feet hurt — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **발**.
Compounds: **발가락** (balgarak) = toe (foot-branch); **발목** (balmok) = ankle (foot-neck).
Related: **맨발** (maenbal) = bare feet (lit. plain-feet); **발바닥** (balbadak) = sole of the foot.

**발가락** (balgarak) = toe — compound: **발** (bal, foot) + **가락** (garak, slender appendage).
Parallel to **손가락** (songarak, finger): the **가락** root applies to both fingers and toes.
**부딪히다** (budichiда) = to bump into/stub — passive form of **부딪다** (to bump).
**발톱** (baltop) = toenail (lit. foot-claw); **손톱** (sontop) = fingernail (lit. hand-claw).

**배** (bae) = stomach/belly/abdomen — pure Korean; also means 'ship/boat' and 'pear' (homonyms).
**배가 아파요** = my stomach hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **배**.
The internal organ (stomach) is **위** (wi, 胃) in medical/Sino-Korean; **배** is the colloquial term.
Related: **배가 고프다** (bae-ga gopda) = to be hungry (lit. stomach is empty).

**몸** (mom) = body — pure Korean noun; used in everyday speech.
The phrase uses **인체** (inche, 人體) = human body — Sino-Korean, more formal/scientific.
**몸이 좋다/나쁘다** = to feel well/unwell (lit. body is good/bad) — common health expression.
Related: **몸무게** (mommuge) = body weight; **몸살** (momsal) = body ache (lit. body-flesh pain).

**심장** (simjang) is Sino-Korean: 心臟 — the physical heart organ.
For emotional 'heart', use **마음** (maeum) = heart/mind (pure Korean).
**심장이 뛰다** = heart is beating — **뛰다** (ttwida) = to beat/jump/run.
**빨리** (ppalli) = quickly/fast — common adverb; **심장이 빨리 뛰어요** = heart is beating fast.

**근육** (geunyuk) is Sino-Korean: 筋肉 — muscle/musculature.
**근육을 다치다** = to injure a muscle — **다치다** (dachida) = to get hurt/injured.
**다쳤어요** = was injured (past tense): **다치다** + **었어요** → **다쳤어요**.
Related: **근육통** (geunyuktong) = muscle pain/soreness; **통** (通/痛) = pain/ache (Sino-Korean suffix).

**피부** (pibu) is Sino-Korean: 皮膚 — skin (the standard word in both everyday and medical use).
**피부가 부드럽다** = skin is soft — **부드럽다** (budeureopda) = to be soft → **부드러워요** (ㅂ irregular).
**피부과** (pibugwa) = dermatology clinic — **과** (科) = department/specialty (Sino-Korean).
Related: **피부색** (pibusaek) = skin color/complexion; **살** (sal) = flesh/skin (pure Korean, informal).

**피** (pi) = blood — pure Korean noun.
The medical/formal term is **혈액** (hyeolaek, 血液) — Sino-Korean, used in clinical contexts.
**헌혈하다** (heonhyeolhada) = to donate blood — **헌** (heon, 獻) = to donate; **혈** (hyeol, 血) = blood.
**피가 나다** = blood comes out (to bleed); **피를 흘리다** = to shed blood.

**뇌** (noe) is Sino-Korean: 腦 — brain (both everyday and medical usage).
**뇌는 복잡해요** = the brain is complex — **는** is the topic particle after vowel-final **뇌**.
**복잡하다** (bokjapada) = to be complex/complicated → **복잡해요**.
Related: **뇌졸중** (noejoljung) = stroke; **뇌파** (noepa) = brain waves — common compound words.

**가슴** (gaseum) covers both chest and breast — context determines the specific meaning.
**통증** (tongjeung, 痛症) = pain/ache — Sino-Korean medical term; more clinical than **아픔**.
**통증을 느끼다** = to feel pain — **느끼다** (neukkida) = to feel/sense; **을** is the object particle.
**느꼈어요** = felt (past tense): **느끼다** + **었어요** → **느꼈어요** (ㅣ + 어 contracts).
cards.englishPhrase: She felt pain in her chest.

cards.grammarNote:
**보다** (boda) = to see/look/watch — pure Korean verb.
**보이다** (boida) = to be visible/to appear — passive/spontaneous form of **보다**.
The phrase **선명하게 보여요** = can be seen clearly — **보여요** is the polite form of **보이다**.
**선명하게** (seonmyeonghage) = clearly — adverb from **선명하다** (to be clear/vivid).

**듣다** (deutda) = to hear/listen — pure Korean verb with ㄷ irregular.
**듣다** → **들어요** (deureoyo) in polite speech — ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowels.
Passive/spontaneous: **들리다** (deullida) = to be heard/audible → **들려요** (deullyeoyo).
**들리지 않아요** = cannot be heard — **-지 않다** is the standard negation pattern.

**냄새** (naemse) = smell/scent — pure Korean noun; **맡다** (matda) = to smell (actively sniff).
The phrase uses **냄새가 나다** = a smell comes out — spontaneous sense perception (passive).
**꽃 냄새가 나요** = the flower smell comes/there is a flower scent.
Related: **향기** (hyanggi) = fragrance/aroma (pleasant smell); **악취** (akchwi) = bad smell/stench.

**맛보다** (matboda) = to taste — compound: **맛** (mat, taste) + **보다** (to see/try).
**맛보세요** = please taste — polite imperative: **맛보** + **세요**.
**맛** alone = flavor/taste (noun); **맛있다** (masitda) = to be delicious; **맛없다** = to taste bad.
Related: **미각** (migak, 味覺) = the sense of taste — Sino-Korean medical/formal term.

**만지다** (manjida) = to touch/handle — pure Korean verb.
**만지지 마세요** = please don't touch — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.
**만지다** vs **닿다** (datda): **만지다** = to touch with intent; **닿다** = to come into contact with.
Related: **촉각** (chokgak, 觸覺) = the sense of touch — Sino-Korean; **감촉** (gamchok) = texture/feel.

**숨을 쉬다** (sumeul swida) = to breathe — lit. 'to breathe/rest one's breath'.
**숨** (sum) = breath (noun); **쉬다** (swida) = to rest/breathe; **을** is the object particle.
**쉬세요** = please breathe — **쉬다** + **세요** (polite imperative after vowel-final stem).
Alternative: **호흡하다** (hohupada) = to breathe (Sino-Korean, more formal/medical).

**구부리다** (gubeurida) = to bend/curve — pure Korean verb.
**구부리세요** = please bend — polite imperative: stem **구부리** + **세요**.
**무릎을 구부리다** = to bend one's knees — **을** is the object particle after **무릎**.
Related: **구부러지다** (gubureojida) = to be bent/curved (intransitive/passive form).

**늘이다** (neurida) = to stretch/lengthen — pure Korean verb (transitive).
The phrase uses **뻗다** (ppeotda) = to extend/stretch out — more natural for extending limbs.
**팔을 쭉 뻗으세요** = please stretch your arms straight — **쭉** = fully/straight (adverb).
**뻗으세요** = please stretch — **뻗다** + **으세요** (polite imperative after consonant-final stem).

**땀을 흘리다** = to sweat — lit. 'to shed/flow sweat'; **땀** (ttam) = sweat; **흘리다** = to spill/shed.
**흘리다** is used for liquids flowing: **눈물을 흘리다** = to shed tears; **피를 흘리다** = to shed blood.
**달릴 때** = when running — **-ㄹ/을 때** expresses 'when [doing something]'.
Related: **땀띠** (ttamddi) = heat rash; **식은땀** (sigeun-ttam) = cold sweat.

**느끼다** (neukkida) = to feel/sense — pure Korean verb.
**기분이 어때요?** = How do you feel? — lit. 'how is your mood?' — uses **기분** + **이/가** + state question.
**어때요** (eottaeyo) = how is it? — from **어떻다** (eotteohda), a common question form.
Related: **느낌** (neukkum) = feeling/sense/impression (noun form of **느끼다**).

**생각하다** (saenggakhada) = to think — **생각** (saenggak, thought/idea) + **하다**.
**생각하고 있어요** = is thinking — **-고 있다** is the progressive pattern (to be doing).
**무슨 생각** = what thought/what are you thinking — **무슨** (museun) = what kind of.
Related: **생각나다** (saenggaknada) = to come to mind; **생각하다** vs **생각나다** is active vs. spontaneous.

**움직이다** (umjigida) = to move — pure Korean verb.
**팔을 움직일 수 없어요** = I can't move my arm — **-ㄹ/을 수 없다** = cannot (lit. 'there is no way to').
**움직이다** → **움직여요** (umjigyeoyo) in polite speech.
Related: **움직임** (umjigim) = movement (noun); **꼼짝도 못하다** = cannot move at all (idiomatic).

**부드러운** (budeuroun) is the modifier form of **부드럽다** (budeureopda, to be soft) — ㅂ irregular.
**부드럽다** → **부드러워요** (budeureowoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
**티슈** (tisyu) = tissue — loanword from English; **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **슈**.
Related: **말랑하다** (mallangada) = to be soft/squishy (for squishy textures); **촉촉하다** = to be moist.

**아픈** (apeun) is the modifier form of **아프다** (apeuda, to hurt/be sick) — ㅡ irregular.
**아프다** → **아파요** (apayo) in polite speech (ㅡ drops before 아).
The phrase uses **쑤시다** (ssusida) = to ache/throb — specifically for muscle soreness or dull aching pain.
**근육이 쑤셔요** = muscles ache/are sore — a more specific term than the general **아파요**.

**왼쪽** (oenjjok) = left side — compound: **왼** (oen, left) + **쪽** (jjok, side/direction).
**왼** alone means left; adding **쪽** specifies direction: **왼쪽으로** = to the left.
**왼쪽 무릎** = left knee — **왼쪽** directly modifies the body part as an adjective.
Opposite: **오른쪽** (oreunjjok) = right side; **왼손** (oenson) = left hand; **오른손** = right hand.

**오른쪽** (oreunjjok) = right side — compound: **오른** (oreun, right) + **쪽** (jjok, side/direction).
**오른팔** (oreunpal) = right arm — **오른** directly combines with the body part (no 쪽 needed).
**골절되다** (goljeol-doeda) = to be fractured — **골절** (骨折) is Sino-Korean; **되다** = to become.
**됐어요** = past tense of **되다**: **되다** + **었어요** → **됐어요** (contracted form).

**상체** (sangche) is Sino-Korean: 上體 — upper body; lit. 'upper-body'.
**상** (上) = upper/above; **체** (體) = body — common in anatomical compounds.
Opposite: **하체** (hache, 下體) = lower body; **전신** (jeonsin) = whole body.
**강하다** (ganghada) = to be strong — **강해요** (ganghaeyo) in polite speech.

**하체** (hache) is Sino-Korean: 下體 — lower body; **하** (下) = lower/below; **체** (體) = body.
The phrase uses **허리가 아파요** for lower back pain — **허리** is more specific than **하체**.
**요통** (yotong, 腰痛) = lower back pain — Sino-Korean medical term: **요** (腰, waist) + **통** (痛, pain).
Related: **하체 운동** (hache undong) = lower body exercise; **다리** and **발** are parts of **하체**.
